info.name: Production-tier matrix (Slice B - ADR 0030 §1-4 + ADR 0032)
info.description:
The tier decides how deep oversight goes. An operator-managed `env` tag on the governing root is carried to child decisions as input.resource.root_attributes (three distinguishable states, ADR 0032); the widened supervisor role opens contents by DIRECT grant; two provenance-scoped `denied` clauses per leaf policy close the production and unproven tiers. Asserted on EXACT ids, counts and error codes through the gateway.

Runs in ORDER. E4 is deliberately LAST: it flips the staging catalog's tier through the operator endpoint, and every earlier cell depends on the original tagging (it flips back, but a failure mid-cell would leave it promoted).

The E4 cells address the CATALOG SERVICE directly ({{catalog_service}}), not the gateway: the operator path is in-network only and the gateway 404s /internal/* at the edge.

item.name: Matrix
E1a — sup-anna lists the STAGING catalog's categories -> 200, exact ids

exec: // The headline of slice B: a supervisor whose reach is derived from the reporting structure
// now opens CONTENTS — because the governing root is tagged env=staging and the role was
// widened to name the child types (a DIRECT grant; inheritance stays confined, ADR 0031).
pm.test('E1a 200 OK', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const body = pm.response.json();
const ids = body.items.map(i => i.id);
pm.test('E1a exactly one category', () => pm.expect(body.count).to.eql(1));
pm.test('E1a and it is the seeded one, by id', () =>
pm.expect(ids).to.eql([pm.environment.get('staging_category_id')]));

pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.environment.get('staging_category_id')));

item.name: E7a — the _actions OMISSION contract: anna's category rows carry no map at all

exec: // The pinned B contract (00-DESIGN §5). The action-enrichment bulk path builds per-row inputs
// with NO root context, so the absent-root deny turns every verb false and the shipped
// omit-on-all-false convention omits the map entirely. OMITTED, never a fabricated
// `view:false` on a row this same matrix just read at 200 (E1b). Threading root context
// through the advice is slice C's work; until then this is the contract, asserted.
pm.test('E7a 200 OK', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const rows = pm.response.json().items;
pm.test('E7a there is a row to judge', () => pm.expect(rows.length).to.eql(1));
rows.forEach((row, i) => pm.test(`E7a row ${i} has NO _actions key`, () =>
pm.expect(row).to.not.have.property('_actions')));

item.name: E7b — the same omission on anna's product rows

exec: pm.test('E7b 200 OK', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const rows = pm.response.json().items;
pm.test('E7b there is a row to judge', () => pm.expect(rows.length).to.eql(1));
rows.forEach((row, i) => pm.test(`E7b row ${i} has NO _actions key`, () =>
pm.expect(row).to.not.have.property('_actions')));

item.name: E2pre — the deny below is the TIER, not a missing role: anna reads the production catalog -> 200

exec: // The anti-vacuity cell. Every E2 assertion below is a 403, and a 403 is also what anna would
// get if her supervised reach to THIS catalog were simply broken — the fixture bootstrap having
// half-failed, say. Root metadata stays ungated (ADR 0030 §1), so a 200 here proves the role is
// resolved and the reach is live, which is what makes the four denials below mean the tier.
pm.test('E2pre 200 OK — the supervised reach is live', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('E2pre it is the production catalog', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.environment.get('prod_catalog_id')));

item.name: E2a — PRODUCTION contents closed: anna lists that catalog's categories -> 403

exec: // The same request as E1a against a root the operator tagged env=production. The decision
// lands at the COARSE type-level gate — nothing tier-related ever enters the SQL residual.
pm.test('E2a the category LIST is DENIED (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));
// A PLAIN deny in slice B: indistinguishable on the wire from any other deny. The structured
// deny_reason and the RFC 9470 challenge are slice C — asserting their ABSENCE here is what
// keeps B's envelope diff at zero.
pm.test('E2a no deny_reason in the body (slice C owns that field)', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.text()).to.not.include('deny_reason'));
pm.test('E2a the ordinary error code', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().errorCode).to.eql('ACCESS_DENIED'));

item.name: E2b — anna GETs a category under the PRODUCTION catalog -> 403

exec: pm.test('E2b the category READ is DENIED (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E2c — anna lists the PRODUCTION catalog's products -> 403

exec: pm.test('E2c the product LIST is DENIED (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E2d — anna GETs a product under the PRODUCTION catalog -> 403

exec: pm.test('E2d the product READ is DENIED (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E6a — MEMBERS UNAFFECTED: the owner reads the PRODUCTION catalog's categories -> 200

exec: // The exact request E2a was denied, by a subject whose role carries provenance=membership.
// Both tier clauses require provenance == 'supervised', so a membership decision cannot
// REACH them — that is ADR 0030 §2, asserted rather than assumed.
pm.test('E6a 200 OK', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const body = pm.response.json();
pm.test('E6a the member sees the row', () => pm.expect(body.count).to.eql(1));
const row = body.items[0];
// And the member's affordance map is PRESENT and honest — the omission E7 pins is scoped to
// the supervised path, not a global regression of the enrichment.
pm.test('E6a _actions is PRESENT on the member row', () =>
pm.expect(row).to.have.property('_actions'));
pm.test('E6a view:true', () => pm.expect(row._actions.view).to.eql(true));
pm.test('E6a update:true (the owner really can write)', () =>
pm.expect(row._actions.update).to.eql(true));

item.name: E3a — UNTAGGED defaults open: anna lists an untagged catalog's categories -> 200, exact ids

exec: // ADR 0030 §3: an untagged root arrives as `{}` — PRESENT and empty, which is a different
// state from absent (enrichment failed). Neither tier clause fires, so contents open. This
// default is defensible only while `env` has no public write path — which E5 proves.
pm.test('E3a 200 OK', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
const body = pm.response.json();
pm.test('E3a exactly one category', () => pm.expect(body.count).to.eql(1));
pm.test('E3a and it is the seeded one, by id', () =>
pm.expect(body.items.map(i => i.id)).to.eql([pm.environment.get('untagged_category_id')]));

item.name: E5a — UNSTRIPPABLE: the OWNER strips env from their own catalog -> 409 TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED

exec: // The subject here is the catalog's own OWNER — the most privileged public identity there is.
// A catalog write is a full-map replace, so submitting no tags over a row carrying `env` IS a
// strip, and the delta check rejects it. Asserted BY CODE, not merely by status: the whole
// reason a new error code exists is that the cell must name WHICH guard fired.
pm.test('E5a the strip is REJECTED (409)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(409));
pm.test('E5a and it names the operator-managed guard', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().errorCode).to.eql('TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED'));

item.name: E5b — the owner RE-VALUES env (production -> dev) -> 409 TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED

exec: pm.test('E5b the re-value is REJECTED (409)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(409));
pm.test('E5b and it names the operator-managed guard', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().errorCode).to.eql('TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED'));

item.name: E5c — the owner ASSIGNS env on the untagged catalog -> 409 TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED

exec: // The third move: an owner cannot promote their own catalog INTO a tier either. Assign,
// re-value and strip are all delta moves on an operator-managed key, and all three close.
pm.test('E5c the assign is REJECTED (409)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(409));
pm.test('E5c and it names the operator-managed guard', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().errorCode).to.eql('TAG_OPERATOR_MANAGED'));

item.name: E5d — ...and none of it moved the tier: the production catalog is still closed to anna

exec: // A rejected write that still changed state would be the quiet failure this cell exists to
// exclude — E5a-c must be rejections, not partial applications.
pm.test('E5d the production tier still holds (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E5e — and the OPERATOR path itself is unreachable through the gateway -> 404

exec: // The other half of 'operator-managed end to end'. E4 writes the tier through the catalog
// service's own port; this cell proves the same request cannot arrive from outside. APISIX
// carries a positive `internal-blocked` route at priority 70 that 404s every /internal/* path,
// above the catalog catch-all — so the in-network-only posture is ENFORCED, not merely intended.
pm.test('E5e the gateway does not route /internal/* (404)', () =>
pm.response.to.have.status(404));

item.name: E4a — the OPERATOR flips the staging catalog to production (in-network only)

exec: // The only write path there is. It reaches the catalog service's published port DIRECTLY:
// the gateway carries a positive `internal-blocked` route that 404s every /internal/* path at
// the edge, which is what makes 'in-network only' enforced rather than intended.
pm.test('E4a the operator write succeeds (200)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('E4a and the merged map carries the new tier', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().env).to.eql('production'));

item.name: E4b — LIVENESS: anna's VERY NEXT child read on that catalog -> 403

exec: // The B analogue of slice A's E4. No re-login, no cache flush, no pod restart: the tier is
// read from the governing root on every request, so the very next one is decided by the new
// state. This is the same request E1b answered 200 a moment ago.
pm.test('E4b the flip is live on the next request (403)', () =>
pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E4c — and the list closes with it -> 403

exec: pm.test('E4c the list closes too (403)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));

item.name: E4d — the operator flips it BACK to staging

exec: pm.test('E4d the operator write succeeds (200)', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('E4d and the tier is staging again', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().env).to.eql('staging'));

item.name: E4e — anna's next read opens again -> 200 (the flip is live in BOTH directions)

exec: // Liveness in one direction only would be indistinguishable from a one-way latch. Closing on
// promotion AND opening on demotion is what shows the decision is read per request.
pm.test('E4e 200 OK again', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('E4e it is the seeded category', () =>
pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.environment.get('staging_category_id')));
